title: The French New Wave
subject: art
description: Young critics at *Cahiers du cinéma* stepped behind the camera. Between **1959** and **1968**, the New Wave freed film from the studio and invented modern auteur cinema.

hero.hook: Film critics grabbed the cameras and reinvented the seventh art.

blocks.text: The **French New Wave** (1959-1968) was not just a style. It was a takeover. Young French cinephiles found studio cinema too stiff, too polished, too written in advance. They wanted to shoot the way you write a novel: freely, in the first person.
By moving from criticism to directing, they made the director the true author of the film. And they changed cinema worldwide.

Before the sound stages there was a magazine, **Cahiers du cinéma**, founded in **1951** by [[André Bazin]]. Around him gathered young critics: **Jean-Luc Godard**, **François Truffaut**, **Claude Chabrol**, **Jacques Rivette**, and **Éric Rohmer**. Their central idea had a name: [[Auteur theory]].

blocks.caption: Cahiers du cinéma: the school where the New Wave learned to think about film

blocks.text: For them, the real creator is not the screenwriter but the one who stages the scene. Framing, rhythm, cuts: that is an author's signature, just as style is a novelist's.

sections.title: 1959: Truffaut and Godard take the stage

blocks.text: In **1959**, **François Truffaut**'s *The 400 Blows* triumphed at Cannes. The film follows **Antoine Doinel**, a teenager coming apart, played by [[Jean-Pierre Léaud]]. The camera follows a life rather than a tight script. The final look straight at us crosses the [[fourth wall]]: the hero stares at the audience, and there is no happy ending.

blocks.caption: Antoine Doinel facing the sea: a young life refusing a fixed destiny

blocks.text: The next year, Godard's *Breathless*, with [[Jean-Paul Belmondo]], shocked audiences with its abrupt cuts. Godard cuts in the middle of a gesture, as if he were writing with scissors.
These two films proved you could tell a story another way: faster, freer, closer to the street.

sections.title: Out of the studio, filming Paris

blocks.text: The break was technical as well. [[Éclair Caméflex]] cameras and faster film stocks made [[Shooting on location and the lightweight camera]] possible. No more heavy studios: they shot in cafes, in apartments, in the streets of Paris, often by natural light.

The actors improvised. Speech became casual, sometimes stumbling. Cinema breathed like life. That freedom later inspired [[Cinema Novo]] in Brazil, then rules as strict as [[Dogme 95]] in Denmark, distant heirs of the same thirst for the authentic.

In the **1970s**, the **New Hollywood** drew on it: **Martin Scorsese**, **Francis Ford Coppola**, and **Steven Spielberg** mixed American efficiency with French freedom. The New Wave left one lasting idea: a film can carry the voice of a single person.

events.title: Cahiers du cinéma
events.detail: The magazine became the laboratory of ideas.

events.title: The 400 Blows
events.detail: Truffaut brought auteur cinema to Cannes.

blocks.text: The New Wave took cinema out of the studio and threw it into the street. It made the director an author, and that idea still shapes independent film all over the world.
